title: Understanding and reducing how patient generated images can distort what clinicians see in remote consultations (SEE-SAFE)
official: SEE-SAFE: Understanding and reducing visual distortion in patient-generated image transfer and video consultations: the effect of device, lighting and software processing on clinician recognition, diagnostic agreement, confidence and triage decisions in adults with visible clinical signs; analysis of patient safety incident reports involving video consultations or shared images; and co-production of standards and guidance with system-level stakeholders
summary:
Background and study aims
Clinicians increasingly assess patients through video calls and through photographs that patients send from their own smartphones. These images do not always show what the patient really looks like. Poor lighting, camera quality, slow internet connections, phone filters and automatic image processing can change colours and hide detail. This could lead a clinician to miss signs such as yellow eyes (jaundice), blue lips (low oxygen) or a rash. These risks may be greater for people with darker skin. At present there are no agreed minimum standards for the quality of images used in remote consultations. SEE-SAFE aims to find out how much images and video are distorted, whether this affects clinicians' decisions, what has gone wrong in real NHS incidents, and to develop practical standards and guidance with patients, clinicians, policy makers, regulators and industry.

Who can participate?
The study has three parts. In Part 1, adults living in Wales who have a confirmed diagnosis of one of four conditions that cause visible signs, who currently show those signs, and who are clinically stable, can take part. A panel of 12 clinicians (GPs and Advanced Practitioners) will also look at the images. Part 2 uses anonymised incident reports and does not recruit anyone. In Part 3, adults aged 18 or over in senior roles in policy, regulation, clinical leadership, commissioning and service delivery, industry or patient advocacy can take part in interviews and a workshop, in English or Welsh.

What does the study involve?
Part 1: participants attend one session lasting about 2 to 3 hours at an NHS outpatient department in North Wales, or are visited at home if they cannot travel. A healthcare assistant supports them and measures their oxygen level. Photographs and video are taken with a range of smartphones and tablets under different lighting conditions. The session is separate from any clinical care and does not change any treatment. Clinicians then view the images and record what they can see and how confident they are. Computer analysis measures how much the images are distorted.
Part 2: researchers will code up to 6,000 anonymised patient safety incident reports about video consultations or shared images, held by NHS England, to describe what happened and why.
Part 3: about 20 stakeholders will be interviewed once, for 45 to 60 minutes, by video call, telephone or in person. Interviewees and other invited stakeholders will then be asked to a workshop to discuss the findings and help write standards, checklists and guidance. Later meetings with organisations will help refine and test these outputs but will not be analysed as research data.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no direct benefit to participants, but the results should help make remote care safer and fairer. Part 1 participants can ask for a summary of the findings and are paid at the NIHR rate for their time with travel costs covered. Part 3 participants receive no payment for their time in a professional capacity; travel expenses are reimbursed. The risks are small: time, tiredness during the photography session, and possible discomfort discussing sensitive organisational issues. Participants can stop at any time. In the workshop, confidentiality cannot be guaranteed because discussion takes place in a group.

Where is the study run from?
Bangor University (North Wales Medical School), working with Cardiff University, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board and other partners.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
December 2026 to September 2028. 

Who is funding the study?
Health and Care Research Wales (Integrated Funding Scheme Call 5).

Who is the main contact?
Dr Rebecca Payne, Bangor University, rebecca.payne@bangor.ac.uk
conditions: Visual distortion of clinical images and video in remote consultations and its effect on patient safety. WP1 focuses on conditions with colour-based visible signs where we will work with our patient advisory group to identify relevant conditions.

interventions.name: SEE-SAFE is a 24-month mixed-methods observational study with three linked work packages (WP), comprising (WP1) an experimental imaging study with clinician assessment of images against reference standards, (WP2) a retrospective cross-sectional analysis of anonymised patient safety incident reports,

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
WP1 (patient participants):
1. Adult (18 years or over) living in Wales.
2. Confirmed diagnosis of one of the four target conditions.
3. Visible clinical signs of the condition at the time of participation.
4. Clinically stable at the time of participation.

WP1 (clinician panel):  
GPs and Advanced Practitioners recruited from North Wales GP Out of Hours services with more than 2 years experience

WP2 (incident reports):
1. Report meets the definition of a patient safety incident (any unintended or unexpected incident which could have, or did, lead to harm for one or more patients receiving healthcare)
2. The consultation involved a video consultation or images shared with a doctor
3. The report contains sufficient information to determine what happened and the aetiology and type of the incident

WP3 (stakeholders):
1. Holds, or has held within approximately the previous three years, a senior role enabling influence over policy, regulation, service delivery, commissioning, professional standards, industry practice or patient advocacy relevant to image-enabled remote healthcare
2. Has experience or a perspective judged, through stakeholder mapping, to be relevant to implementation of standards and guidance
3. Can contribute system-level insight into how evidence is interpreted, prioritised or operationalised
4. Aged 18 years or over, and able and willing to provide informed consent
5. Can participate in English or Welsh
Exclusion criteria:
WP1:
1. Clinically unwell at the time of participation
2. Lacks capacity to consent
3. Participation would pose a risk to wellbeing

WP3:
1. No credible current or recent route to influence policy or practice in this area
2. Unable to provide informed consent
3. Direct involvement creates an unmanaged conflict of interest that would make participation inappropriate (reviewed by the Chief Investigator and documented)

WP2: 
None beyond failing the inclusion criteria
